scenario: A 19-year-old sexually active woman has 4 days of lower abdominal pain. She uses condoms inconsistently. Temperature is 37.4 C (99.3 F). Urine hCG is negative. There is no vomiting, peritoneal sign, or palpable mass. Her examination is otherwise being completed, and nucleic acid amplification tests for gonorrhea and chlamydia are sent; results will take 2 days. No other cause of her pain is identified.
question: Which of the following findings on pelvic examination is, by itself, sufficient to begin empiric treatment for pelvic inflammatory disease?
options: {"options": ["A palpable tender adnexal mass", "Oral temperature above 38.3 C (101 F)", "Cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination", "Mucopurulent cervical discharge", "Abundant white blood cells on saline microscopy of vaginal fluid"], "blueprintSystem": "reproductive", "taskCategory": "history-physical", "blueprintTopic": "minimum clinical criteria to start empiric PID treatment", "keyTakeaway": "Cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness alone, in a young woman with pelvic pain and no other cause, is enough to start PID treatment.", "kind": "vignette"}
correctAnswer: Cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination
explanation: Pelvic organ tenderness is correct. The CDC 2021 STI treatment guidelines recommend empiric PID treatment for sexually active young women with pelvic or lower abdominal pain, when no other cause is found, if 1 or more minimum clinical criteria is present on pelvic examination: cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness. A low threshold is used because untreated PID causes infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pain. Fever above 38.3 C, mucopurulent discharge, and abundant vaginal fluid WBCs are additional criteria that increase specificity but are not required. A palpable adnexal mass suggests a tubo-ovarian abscess and needs ultrasonography and usually admission. Treatment should not wait for NAAT results. Takeaway: pelvic pain plus cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness = treat for PID now.

scenario: A 27-year-old woman with polycystic ovary syndrome (oligomenorrhea, clinical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology) has been trying to conceive for 14 months. question: Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic treatment for infertility?

explanation: Letrozole is correct. scenario: A 22-year-old college student has had 14 months of intense fear that she will say something foolish and be judged when she must speak in seminars, eat in the dining hall, or meet new classmates. She blushes and trembles in these situations, avoids them when she can, and has dropped 2 courses that require presentations. She is comfortable with 2 close friends and her family. question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Since his late teens he has believed he can sense other people's thoughts and that license plate numbers carry special messages meant for him, though he concedes these might be coincidences. He wears mismatched, unusual clothing, speaks in vague, overelaborate phrases, and has no close friends apart from his sister. question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

scenario: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by friends after smoking methamphetamine at a party 2 hours ago. He is agitated, talking rapidly, and pacing, and says his heart is racing. He has taken no other drugs or medications, per his friends. question: Which of the following sets of findings is most consistent with his presentation?
options: {"options": ["Miosis, salivation, bronchorrhea, bradycardia, and diarrhea", "Mydriasis, dry flushed skin, urinary retention, and absent bowel sounds", "Normal pupils, slurred speech, ataxia, and normal vital signs", "Mydriasis, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, and hyperthermia", "Lead-pipe rigidity, bradykinesia, and hyperthermia"], "blueprintSystem": "psychiatry", "taskCategory": "history-physical", "blueprintTopic": "physical findings of sympathomimetic (methamphetamine) intoxication", "keyTakeaway": "Sympathomimetic toxidrome: mydriasis, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia; sweating separates it from anticholinergic toxicity.", "kind": "vignette"}
correctAnswer: Mydriasis, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, and hyperthermia
explanation: Mydriasis, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, and hyperthermia are correct. The 2024 ASAM/AAAP stimulant use disorder guideline describes stimulant intoxication as a sympathomimetic syndrome of agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, and dilated pupils, managed first with benzodiazepines, cooling, and a calm setting. Dilated pupils with dry flushed skin, urinary retention, and absent bowel sounds are anticholinergic; sweating distinguishes sympathomimetic toxicity. Miosis with salivation, bronchorrhea, bradycardia, and diarrhea is cholinergic. Slurred speech and ataxia with normal pupils and vital signs suggest sedative-hypnotic or alcohol intoxication. scenario: A 28-year-old man with schizophrenia is brought in by his family after 4 days of not speaking, eating, or drinking. He holds his arms raised in odd postures for long periods, resists passive movement with equal force, and keeps a fixed stare. Temperature is 37.2 C (99 F), pulse is 92/min, blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg, and creatine kinase is normal. He has had no antipsychotic dose change in 6 months. Toxicology screen and basic metabolic panel are unremarkable except for mild hypernatremia, which is being corrected with IV fluids.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
options: {"options": ["Ziprasidone 20 mg IM", "Haloperidol 5 mg IM", "Benztropine 2 mg IV", "Sertraline 50 mg orally daily", "Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV"], "blueprintSystem": "psychiatry", "taskCategory": "pharmacotherapy", "blueprintTopic": "lorazepam for catatonia in schizophrenia", "keyTakeaway": "Catatonia: IV lorazepam 1 to 2 mg first, ECT if no response; avoid adding high-potency antipsychotics.", "kind": "vignette"}
explanation: Lorazepam is correct. The 2020 APA schizophrenia practice guideline notes that catatonia should be treated with a benzodiazepine, typically lorazepam, with ECT if there is no prompt response; an IV lorazepam challenge of 1 to 2 mg often produces rapid improvement and supports the diagnosis. He has mutism, posturing, negativism, and staring, with stable vital signs and normal CK, which argues against NMS. High-potency antipsychotics such as haloperidol can worsen catatonia and increase the risk of NMS, so they should be held during acute catatonia. Ziprasidone carries the same concern. Takeaway: catatonia (mutism, posturing, negativism, staring): give IV lorazepam first and avoid adding antipsychotics; ECT if no response.

scenario: A 28-year-old woman has 2 days of sore throat. She reports subjective fever and fatigue. She asks for a strep test and antibiotics because her coworker had strep throat last month. You are completing her history and examination to decide whether group A streptococcal testing is warranted.
question: Which of the following findings most strongly argues against testing for group A streptococcal pharyngitis?
options: {"options": ["Cough, rhinorrhea, and hoarseness", "Tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy", "Tonsillar exudate", "Palatal petechiae", "Temperature of 38.6 C (101.5 F)"], "blueprintSystem": "eent", "taskCategory": "history-physical", "blueprintTopic": "viral features that argue against testing for group A streptococcal pharyngitis", "keyTakeaway": "Sore throat with cough, rhinorrhea, and hoarseness suggests a virus; GAS testing is not indicated.", "kind": "vignette"}
explanation: Cough, rhinorrhea, and hoarseness are correct. The IDSA 2012 group A streptococcal pharyngitis guideline recommends against testing patients with sore throat whose clinical features, such as cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness, and oral ulcers, strongly suggest a viral cause, because such patients are unlikely to have GAS and testing leads to treatment of carriers. In adults, a negative rapid antigen test needs no backup culture. Tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, fever, and palatal petechiae are features that increase the likelihood of GAS and support testing with a rapid antigen test or culture. scenario: A 15-month-old boy is seen for a well-child visit. He has 8 erupted primary teeth without visible caries or white-spot lesions. He drinks from a bottle at bedtime. question: In addition to anticipatory guidance, which of the following is the most appropriate preventive intervention at this visit?
options: {"options": ["Recommend fluoride-free training toothpaste until age 3", "Wait to apply fluoride until his first dental visit at age 3", "Prescribe chlorhexidine mouth rinse", "Apply fluoride varnish to his primary teeth", "Place dental sealants on the primary molars"], "blueprintSystem": "eent", "taskCategory": "prevention", "blueprintTopic": "fluoride varnish for primary teeth in a toddler", "keyTakeaway": "Apply fluoride varnish to primary teeth starting at eruption; supplement oral fluoride from 6 months if water is deficient.", "kind": "vignette"}

explanation: Fluoride varnish is correct. The 2021 USPSTF dental caries recommendation (grade B) advises primary care clinicians to apply fluoride varnish to the primary teeth of all infants and children starting at primary tooth eruption, and to prescribe oral fluoride supplementation starting at age 6 months for children whose water supply is deficient in fluoride; his well water should be tested.
